sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran, Alvin Harry Wedler. Mr. Wedler served in the U.S. Army with the 125th AAA Gun Battalion, C Battery. He served in the European Theater, and his highest rank was PFC. I'm Tom SWOPE (ph), and this recording was made at Mr. Wedler's home in Burton, Ohio, on August 27th, 2003. Alvin was 78 at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Forty-one, I was living in Cleveland Heights, Ohio, on Taylor Road, and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How old were you?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Eighteen.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Eighteen? Were you out of school?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Well, yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. Do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Yes. I was at Jervaci's (ph) Pool Hall, shooting pool, drinking Coke and eating Clark bars, and the announcement came over the -- the radio. And, of course, I was shocked -- as everyone was -- and, yeah, I do have a memory of that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you tempted to run out there and sign up the next day?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: No. I had no idea that that was happening. The draft was -- was pretty much in -- in effect then, wasn't it?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh, yes.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: And I was 18 at -- actually, that war, in my -- in my mind, was coming years before. It probably spoiled my whole school, because at 15 or so, it was pretty obvious we were going to be engulfed in this war. And I was in high school, and I -- I'll tell you something, my folk -- my dad had a book on World War I, and it was kept out of sight, but I found it. And I opened this book, and there were some pretty horrible pictures in there of people with their legs blown off and without heads, and whatever. And this is the picture that I had in mind; if you went to the army, you were going to end up like that. And I decided that while I was here and a -- and a civilian, and whatever, I was going to have -- I was going to live my life before I got drafted, because once you got in the army, that was the result. So it really tended to mess up my schooling, unfortunately.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when --

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: But, anyhow --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Go ahead. When were you finally called, then?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Oh, gosh, I don't know the exact date.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Doesn't have -- the exact date doesn't matter.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Well, when I was 18 --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. So --

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: -- I -- I had the option of not going because my father had a machine shop, Wedler Manufacturing Company, and it was mentioned that I could get a job, start working down there, and I wouldn't have to worry about the draft. But, like you pointed out before, did you run right out and -- and join up? No, I didn't, but I wouldn't allow that. I was -- I allowed myself to be drafted, and I wanted to go and do my part, so that's what happened. I was drafted and went to Fort Hayes, and from Fort Hayes out to California, and from California back to Louisiana, and Louisiana up to Massachusetts. I got to see the country, all right, and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything interesting or unusual happen during your training?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Everything was unusual in our training. We -- we trained out in California, and we trained as infantry, really. We had infantry training only be -- only to be turned into anti-aircraft work out on Mojave Desert. And with our mill -- 40 -- 90-millimeter guns, and -- it was -- it was tough training. It was hot and -- and hard, but it was to our benefit, really.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was it tough when you first went in to be thrown in with guys from all over the country, different culture kind of thing?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Well, when I first went in, we -- we were together with Ohio ones --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: -- for the most part down at Fort Hayes, but, no, I never had any problem. I didn't have any problem meshing with the -- with the guys. They were all -- we were all in the same boat. What -- what are you going to do, you know. There -- we -- we had no desire to be out, so we were all in there to do a job, and we worked together and got it done.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when were you put in a -- in an anti-aircraft outfit?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Out in California. As soon as we got out to California, we were tested for this or that. Dino (ph), over here, and I ended up in the range section, pretty much based on -- on how you did in your intelligence test. They separated us to do the jobs that we were expected to do. We were -- we were classed as a 9 -- 938, I think, instrument operator, and ended up working with early radar and -- and computer. The computers in those days were radio tube computers -- they didn't have this fancy stuff -- and our computer was encased in a steel trailer. It had a window on one side which was -- had a -- a steel slider on it to slide across, and -- it was interesting. It was interesting work.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So your specific job was in range-finding, kind of thing?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: We would -- our 90-millimeter outfit was set up that we had a tracking head, a visual tracking head with an elevation scope on one side and an azimuth scope on the other, operated by two fellows, and it (slewed) by electricity -- we had a power plant. And they would -- they would get -- they would locate the target, and they'd get their scope on these things, and, of course, track it as it was going along these V-1 bombs, or in practice, the target plane, or whatever. Now, that information from the tracking head was via cable sent to the director, and the director would -- the computer would correct the information that it was receiving at that time and -- and forwarding it 10 or 12 seconds so that you would be pointing the guns at where it was going to be rather than where it was. And that -- that information from a -- from a computer was transported by cable again to four 90- millimeter guns who had an azimuth and elevation dial on the -- on the platform, and they had two sets of pointers. They had the ones that we were transmitting to them, plus the ones that they would operate by hand wheels. And if they matched, they would match pointers, then, and pretty soon these things are both going where that thing is going to be, or predicted to be, with all the ballistic information corrections in there, as far as air density, and whatever. And when the data was smooth, when everything smoothed out, the officer of the day would issue the order to fire and they would start firing at these things. It was pretty interesting. We -- when we got overseas, we were firing at the Buzz Bombs, and when the -- when we started, we just had regular ammunition, and it -- it depended on matching pointers and almost getting a direct hit on it to -- to knock it down or to disable it. Very soon after, over -- over there, we got an ammunition they called "Bonzo Ammunition", and it would -- it would explode when it got within 75 yards of the target, so now we didn't have to be so damn accurate with that. You could see -- and it was interesting, you could -- you could see the -- once we started firing, you could see the bursts going pow, pow, pow, pow, pow, behind the thing. And eventually, you could see that those bursts catch up with it and -- and destroy the target. We were credited -- and I don't think any outfit can match it -- we were credited with knocking down 750 V-1 bombs, either an -- either Cat A, in the air; or Cat B, disabling and letting them come down. I re -- one night, didn't we fire a thousand rounds? I think one -- one night over there we fired a thousand rounds at 40 bucks a piece. I -- we figured that -- somebody told us that they cost 40 dollars a piece to make. That's a lot of -- lot of rounds.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Tell him we fired so many rounds, we had to change the barrels --

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Oh, yeah. We wore out some barrels.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: -- because they were worn out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So where were you set up, then, when you went to England?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Originally, we landed at Liverpool, and we were -- we spent our first nights up around Black Shore Moors (ph), or something, I think they called it. From there, we were -- we trucked on down to the southern coast of England and got the -- on the track of the V-1's that were being fired and directed to London. And that was -- that was an interesting thing, wasn't it, Dino?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: When we were down there, they had -- they had barriers to these V-1's. They were launched from France, and they had to cross the English Channel, of course. When they were crossing the English Channel, the Air Force intercepted them. And it was interesting that the V-1 could go faster than our pursuit planes in those days, and the only way they could catch them was to fly at a high altitude, spot them down below, take a power dive behind them, and level off behind them and -- and let go with their nose cannon. That was their only hope, because they -- they weren't fast enough to catch them. If they missed, then they ran into our anti-aircraft belt. We were -- we were not alone down there. It was our outfit, right beside us was a British combination. Their -- their anti-aircraft was co-educational. They had women and men. And then -- yeah, they couldn't hit the broad side of a barn anyhow, so it's -- it's a good thing we were there. But we'd watch them miss, and then we'd smack them. But if they got past the fighter planes, and then the few that got past us, then from there on, the only thing to stop them were the barrage balloons that they had around London, and those were -- those would -- hopefully, would catch them. But even then, they didn't catch them all. These things carried a 2,000-pound warhead, and it created a hell of a lot of damage. And it was very exciting to fire at these and clip them a little bit and watch them go anywhere they pleased to go on the continent later on. We clipped one one night, and it just went directly -- directly vertically up over us, like that, until it ran out of oomph, and then just flipped over like this, and started to come right down on our outfit. Everybody scrambled and jumped on top of each other and did the -- this was up in Holland -- and got into these irrigation ditches with all the mosquito larva and every other darn thing. Anyhow, before it smacked us, it leveled out like a toy glider. When you were a kid, you know, you'd throw those things. And it went like this, and it hit the hotel behind us in the middle of town, and -- Wouw, W-O-U-W -- and just blew the hell out of it. The building was un-sided, you know. Just blew the walls away, and all you could see were these little rooms. So that -- that was always exciting to do that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So I'm guessing you got to England probably, what, 1944, mid-1944, maybe?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: You know, when something's past me, I kind of forget about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay. Let's put this in relation to D-Day. Before D-Day, or after D-Day?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Oh, it was after D-Day.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: After D-Day? So -- so --

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Sure. We landed -- we landed at Omaha Beach, though, when we --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you -- when you went over to the _____?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: When we finally shipped across, we went over in whatever they had to take us over on, and I think it was a converted Liberty Ship, or something. It took us longer to cross the Channel than it did to cross the ocean because of the weather conditions. You can imagine we had heavy equipment, with our 90-millimeters. It wasn't only the guns, it was the range equipment, radar, and all that stuff. So we had to have some pretty good capacity. And we didn't have any docks to land at at that time, but it wasn't that far along. So we crossed the Channel and rode out at anchor all these rough seas until things calmed down enough that they could make an attempt to unload us, and that wasn't fun. That was -- there wasn't anything -- there wasn't anything going, and all you had to do was sit there and wait. And when -- when we finally did get -- when it finally did get calm enough, they unloaded us on -- on these -- they called them "walruses". They were great big steel-tread raft with two huge outboard motors on the back. Your Evinrudes, and your stuff, they were like that, only 20 times bigger; just huge outboards. And they'd -- they'd tie those off to the ship, and then they'd take their cranes and lift this equipment over and drop it down on those rafts. And so that was our means of getting onto the continent, and we did it. And that was -- that was a sight to behold, too, because the invasion had happened, and there were ships there that they sunk intentionally, and some of them were sunk unintentionally by the enemy, I guess, and to use as break _____, you know. Break walls, they'd protect the beach so that they could land all this equipment, and whatever. Debris, battle debris laying all over the place. It was good. We -- we landed, we went up on higher ground -- a lot easier than the guys did at D-Day, by the way -- and prepared to take up our next position in Cherbourg. We were firing at the V-1's now, before they got to the Channel, and stuff. And from there, we went up into Holland, Wouw. What a name, Wouw, huh?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: And --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What's -- what's Wouw stand for?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: It's the name of a town.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The -- the -- okay.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: W-O-U-W.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: W-O-U-W?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Sounds like a radio station, doesn't it?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I think I worked there once.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: W-O-U-W calling.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: W-O-E-W, Wouw?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: No, W-O-U-W.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: W-O-U-W, in Holland?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wouw.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Wouw.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wouw. So that's where you were set up?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Yeah. We set up up there, and we were there for quite a while. That -- that almost became like a home base for it -- for us, didn't it? Wouw?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: We were there for -- for a -- a while, and we -- well, you -- you -- you just got to form some friendships there in town. And they had people coming in doing laundry for us, and whatever, and we -- our old friends, the Buzz Bombs, again, of course. And we'd work -- we'd be on duty eight hours and off duty 16, wasn't it?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Yeah. We were on, was it, eight hours?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Yeah. Eight-hour shift, and so --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What'd you do during those off-duty times?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Oh, shot crap, and shoot the breeze, and whatever, tried to take up our time. You -- you -- you were never really off duty because you were always under threat of these -- these things. They were firing them one after another. And there was one event there that we heard -- they made a -- they sounded like a Transcontinental truck with no muffler going like hell, and you could hear them from a long way off. And this one evening, we heard this V-1 sound, and we're -- we're watching the radar and it's -- standing around and not -- not finding -- not spotting anything, and sound's getting louder, and now you're starting to look around, where the hell is that thing. And it -- it got really louder, like it was almost upon you, and -- and I looked across the dike, and coming right towards us, spewing up dirt like a motor boat would spew up water, you know, the wake, spraying it up, it was dirt. They had launched this thing on ground level, and it was coming along the ground just like if you'd put a -- a jet boat in the lake, here, spraying the water up, that dirt was going up like this. Well, it was coming, coming, coming, and definitely deafeningly loud, and, boy, you -- you started folks like this, this is it. And the damn thing hit a dike that it wasn't able to blast through, and it clipped it up like this, and went -- that went into -- into Wouw, didn't it? That -- that ground-level one?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: That went into Wouw, blew the hell out of the town. Exciting little things like that that -- that happened. There's a couple of them that you remember, and that -- that was one of them. You'll never forget that, of course. And those darn Limies I was telling you about, shooting at these things, should have seen our tents, you know. You ever been to a -- a display of -- of the stars and everything, and all the lights go out and you look up and you see all these stars? Our tents looked like that from the shrapnel of these damn Limies shooting up there and just missing, of course. But all the -- all the crap from their rounds came down and put holes in our tent. You could lay there and look at the -- study the stars just like this, oh, there's the Big Dipper.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Well, we -- we had an older person in our outfit, and he was good for the job he did. He took care of the power plant and he was always scared _____+ the fox hole, so the guys, you see, try to play tricks on him. So they pick up a piece of shrapnel, throw it in his fox hole, and every time you saw that piece of shrapnel, he'd dig his fox hole deeper. And -- and he got it so deep he couldn't get out of it.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: He was from Akron. He was from Akron. He was kind of a -- nice guy, though. He was in charge of the power plants. Treated them like -- like babies, spotlessly clean, and right up to snuff.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: The power plants ran 24 hours and then you shut it off and start the other one up. In the meantime, when the other one's running, you -- you'd service this one, but they ran 24 hours a day. And we were -- fortunately, we did have electricity --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: -- so we had one radio at -- at our outfit, so everybody bought -- got a speaker and they -- they put wires through the radio, and everybody had music and everything.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: It was my radio.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You brought that with you?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: No, my mother sent it over. It was a little --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: -- little one of those little things like this. You should have seen what that little thing was asked to do, just jumping off the speaker with two wires to two wires to two wires, and it did a job for us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So were you in Wouw when the Battle of the Bulge broke?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: When it broke?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh, when it started?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Yeah. We were in Wouw.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Yeah, I guess we were. Yeah. We had -- we had just -- it seems that we had just come back there not too long before. We -- we had just finished -- they took us away from there for a while. They wanted us -- they had some crazy idea that we could fire the V-2's, and they took us out of Wouw and trucked us down a ways, put us in an old Polish calvary barracks down there position. The -- the Germans were so far ahead of us, really, at that time, that it -- it was -- they didn't know what was going on. Anyhow, so they shipped us down there expecting that we'd set up and shoot at V-2's, until somebody finally realized that that damn V-2 was going faster than our shell was going, you know, the -- so how are we going to shoot down something like that? No. So we spent a little bit of time there. And -- and some of guys enjoyed that, because being a cavalry barracks, they -- they suddenly discovered that they were mating horses in there and they -- we'd have matinees. And we had -- we had our favorite horses come out, you know, like this, and they'd go back like this. Well, you have to do something. So, anyhow, we -- we -- we got out of there, and we were going back to Wouw, and we went up there to Wouw. They were still shooting the V-1's, and we had just -- our radar was -- was like a big over-the-highway trailer. I mean, it had a -- it was bulky. We had just finished digging that in, and our computer trailer, and whatever, and -- and I don't know whether it got to -- to tent floors yet or not -- we always took scraps of things and made floors to our tents eventually -- but we had just finished digging in there, and this Bulge thing came up and we had to leave that and go down to -- to the Bulge. And -- and Tongress (ph) was cold, bitter, bitter cold. It was -- I don't suppose they'll get in trouble anymore, but my parents -- my dad used to take a sip of Golden Wedding every evening when he'd come back from his work. And in one of these packages that came by mail, I take this out and that, and the letter, and the -- the cookies and everything, down in the bottom was this bottle, this pint bottle of Golden Wedding. And, boy, because it was cold as hell, well, you -- you'd share that with people that you're close to. Dino didn't drink a drop, I don't think, he -- but other friends of mine there did, so I had it. They were all freezing and, here, you want a slug? Yeah, sure. Well, it didn't last long. A pint doesn't go around -- go around too many times. I was put on guard duty right away. We were guarding a -- a -- not an ammunition dump, but a gasoline dump supply, and I was on guard duty out there. It was cold, bitter cold. Well, that bottle finally got drained, and the -- but I got off guard duty, somebody else relieved me, and it was time to get something to eat. They set up some kind of a chow line, and one of our cooks -- I'm going through there with my _____+ getting this and that, and I'm going around there, and all of a sudden _____ goes like this, you know, right _____. And I looked at him, was -- was Diamato (ph). Diamato took a swing at me right -- right across the table. Took a swing at me, and I said, Joe, what the hell's going on. He says, you son of a gun, he says. I know, he says, you had a bottle and you didn't even give me a sip of it. You did, honest to God. Surprised the hell out of me, too. So, anyhow, that's little experiences that you remember that are -- that are kind of fun. We opened up on a -- that squadron, a flight of Thunderbolts. We -- we had a West Point lieutenant on duty. He was off for the day, and here comes these Thunderbolts coming. Well, they flashed the I.F.F., Identification Friend or Foe, and we flashed up to them. Got no answer, so old Lieutenant Wicker (ph) at that time gave the order of fire. We -- we fired a -- after the first burst, these Thunderbolts are like this, you know. We never hit anything. But he was a West Point lieutenant, and he got his file lifted out and put to the rear again. He's a lieutenant, he's still alive. He's in a -- some kind of an -- an officer's retirement home up around Washington. He's a lieutenant colonel. But that was a terrible embarrassment to him, because he -- he screwed up. But he didn't screw up, you know. It was perfectly logical what he did. If he hadn't done that, they'd probably turned out to be Germans flying our planes, and they'd probably come down and strafed us, and whatever. But it wasn't that way, but nobody knew that at the time. So there's been some neat things. We still have -- our battery commander is still living, and he comes to our reunions every summer, or had come, and he -- and he fully intends to come to -- to our gathering, now that it's a gathering. But that worked out. That gathering, that worked out very well, because instead of having a lot of long faces down there this past July -- July after -- it -- it -- it was always a tough thing when the reunion ended to say so-long to some of these guys, because you didn't know whether you were going to see them again or not. But this one would have been doubly depressing, because you knew you weren't going to see them again if there -- if it wasn't to continue. So it was very nice to look around and see everybody with a smile on their face, because they had something still to look forward to that they could take part in -- or not. That their choice, not that they were closed off from finally, just slam the door, so --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have any other memories from the Battle of the Bulge?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: We never fired a shot down there. The -- Dino and I were both at a city called Comblayopon (ph), and it was the -- there was the Meuse River was coming right through this town, and that bridge that was going across the river there, we were supposed to defend to -- to our death if we had to. And we could hear it. We could hear these battle -- this is going on. The -- that was where the Germans ran out of gas, and they ran out of gas three miles from us, so -- but we were prepared to do what we were asked to do, and thank God we didn't have to do that, you know; that -- that something stopped them before we had to. But they weren't going to -- the bridge was all -- all mined to be destroyed, and we had -- we had some German aircraft dropping flares at us that turned -- we thought we were all secure under the night sky, you know, and all these flares come down, and, boy, it was just like daylight or better. That -- that was a little disconcerting, but we were there. We had -- there were four of our 90s. We only had one 90 at -- at our town, didn't we?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: One -- one 90.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: One gun at each crossroad --

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Yeah. And we were having to stop everyone, all truck traffic, car traffic, and walking traffic, and ask them for our -- for their -- for their identification, and --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: You should tell him we went through Lyase (ph), there was Buzz Bombs coming down all over --

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: -- and one of them came down, hit one of the guns. An M-4 tractor, it demolished. 15 guys were killed.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Yeah. That was -- that was our loss.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: It was at night, and we -- we had to stop outside of Lyase, and the colonel had to talk to the captain. And the colonel said to the captain, he said, one gun at each crossroad. And you have no protection. So we expect Tiger Tanks tomorrow night, and you don't shoot on them until they're real close. And you can't shoot them from the front, you have to shoot them from the side, otherwise you won't do anything to them. And when your guns are all wiped out, everybody's on their own, so -- but the Tiger Tanks never got to us.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: They ran out of gas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Ran out of gas?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: That was quite a machine. That was quite a fighting machine, that Tiger Tank. I'll tell you something, that the -- well, of course, the Germans knew what they -- what they were going to be getting into, so that they -- they had a chance to develop this stuff and -- that we were unaware of, but I went on furlough -- well, that Tiger Tank is one thing. I mean, that was so much better than anything we had. The -- the V-1 and the V-2, of course, they were still getting information from that and using it, but what really got me, I -- we had our choice -- we -- we were turned into MP's after this thing was over. We were to process guys and send them down to the -- the (?Easternary's?) Theater, or whatever, and we had a chance for furloughs finally when we were in this position. And we had our choice of going to Switzerland, or England, or whatever. Well, I'd become so sick and tired of people jibber-jabbering on the street and not being able to understand whether they were complementing you or rappin' ya, but I -- I chose to go to England where I could understand people, so I did. A guy that was on the guns who -- you know, you're in different sections in these outfits, and you tend to -- to socialize with people that are close to you rather than the ones that are not, and this -- this guy was on the guns. And, of course, we were all pals and buddies and friends, but somehow or other, I -- I got this opportunity to go to England. And this guy on the guns, his name was Burrier (ph), chose the same thing, so we -- we decided we'd go together. And never buddy-buddied in the outfit, and we had a hell of a good time. But we went over there and we went -- we went through Hyde Park, and they had a -- a display of -- of captured aircraft, and they had a Liberator Bomber of ours, and they had a Flying Fortress of ours, and -- and here around the corner, they had this aircraft I hadn't seen the likes of. And it turned out to be a Messerschmitt, a jet-propelled Messerschmitt sitting there that they had captured. And when you read about it, it -- it was -- it was used in action. I mean, it was used. We never -- we didn't have a damn jet fighter, and here these guys, what's this? This is a reality. This isn't a piece of paper and drawing, this is -- this is actually, here it is. Well, if you got over that, down the line a little bit, here's a rocket plane. They had a rocket plane sitting right there, actually touch it, feel it, it's a reality, too. We're still flying Mustangs, and stuff. That was close, you know that? It was very close that we did not win that war. And I just couldn't believe the -- how far along they were, and how relatively far behind we were. But we out-produced them, and, of course, it's pretty hard to produce rocket planes from a bombed-out factory, and whatever. So our -- those -- didn't that -- didn't that awe you when we were in on the southern coast of England, seeing those Flying Fortresses going over? They'd fly at real high altitudes, and you'd go over there and it was just wave after wave of planes going just about that fast -- they looked like they were going that fast -- just as far either side as you could see, and as far back and forward. And they're just going there. It was -- it was just hard to imagine how anybody could survive an attack like that, it was just wave after wave after wave. It was -- it was kind of -- being on our side, it was kind of nice to see, but, boy, hard to believe. It's just -- even today, it's hard to imagine that what you saw, you really saw. But you did, and it was there. And we get together once a year and talk about it, and every -- the other guys have seen it, too, so I guess it wasn't a dream, but it seems almost like a dream. Doesn't it seem like a dream sometimes?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: You should also tell him about why we missed the Thunderbolts. Otherwise, they'll think that we're not a straight shooter.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Oh, I told him about that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Why he missed them?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Well, I told -- as soon as one burst was up there, they just went pow --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: No, that wasn't the reason. The reason was the day before we had to check our instruments, and when you check them, you put everything to zero. You turn all your dials to zero --

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Oh, I don't know about this.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: -- to check it. And then they forgot to put it all back in, because the computer's one -- in one place, the guns are so many yards to the -- in front of you, and you have to allow for that. So you put that in your computer, and they forgot to -- to put it all back in, and that's why we missed them.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Gee, I didn't know that story. I thought I knew everything.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: It's a good thing that they -- they forgot to do that, otherwise we would have hit them.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Well, we'd a hit one, anyhow.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have any close buddies over there?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Over where?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Overseas?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Close buddies now, do we have any close --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Over back -- when you -- during the war. You can introduce your --

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Oh, oh, oh, oh, yeah. I got -- Dino was right beside me.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Dino was right beside you?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Yes. He knows the story of -- of not putting that -- those --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did -- what did you guys do for fun, if -- well, I'm sure there wasn't much time for fun, but for relaxation between, when you were off duty?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Well, I probably drank, but Dino --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: I was different, though.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: We lived two different lives over there.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: I -- I didn't go out too much.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Used to visit the night clubs over there.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: I used to play in them. I play the drums, and -- or, I did, and they'd allow us to jam with them. And there were a couple of cafes in Nijlen -- how do you spell Nijlen? N-I-J --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Oh, god, I -- A -- L-E-N, something like that. Anyway, that was in Belgium, and when -- we were firing at the V-1's directed to Antwerp, and we had -- a nice little town. It was a nice little town. Had -- it had a cafe that had collaborated with the Germans, and it was -- it was called the Red -- Red Door. It had a glass door that they had painted red, and it -- it kind of glowed just like there was light behind it, but it didn't emit any light. And we were -- that was supposed to be off-limits to us. Then right beside that was a -- a place that we called the Glass Roof -- oh, no, I'm sorry, the Corner Cafe, and then a block down that way was the Glass Roof, and -- and one down here by the theater that we had, they had dances down there for us at one time. We called that one Keyboomps (ph), and -- I'll tell you a funny story about that Corner Cafe. We -- my buddy, who lives down on Psalm Center (ph) is a -- is a musician. I mean, he -- he plays the violin. He's -- he's good. So we -- we patronized this Corner Cafe and got real friendly with the -- they had a guy named Zeus that played the accordion, I think, and -- and Louie played the trumpet, and they had a -- I forget the drummer's name, but anyhow, I replaced him, and we got real friendly with those guys. So one night when we closed the place up -- we weren't out on duty -- and ready to make our way back to our camp, this -- this Esborn (ph) guy, called him Essie, Essie and I stepped out of the Corner Cafe and we started walking back to camp -- as best we could, you know. Then all of a sudden we passed the -- the Red Door, and it was okay. And Essie decided that he wanted to kick that door in because they're a bunch of collaborators anyhow, so -- I didn't do it, Dear, it wasn't me. Anyhow, he takes his foot and he goes like that, and then it broke the glass. We didn't want any more trouble, so we just kept walking. But Essie had a guilty conscience and he imagined that people were following us from that place. He had -- he had gotten a hold of a -- some Canadian commando's knife, and it was -- it was a dagger. It was -- probably had a blade that long, and a sharp stiletto point on the thing, and ground sides. It was neat. And it -- Essie carried that on his waist around -- under his belt. So he pulls this knife out a little, you know, something like, let them come, or whatever. (END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE; BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE) Turned out to be Louie and Zeus from the Corner Cafe that were behind us, so he didn't need this knife anymore. So he nudges me like this, and he says, you know, he says, I'll bet you I can put this knife back in this sheath without even looking. Honest to God. I said, oh, I don't know. I don't know that you should do that. Ah, he says, I can do this without even looking, watch. And he goes woomp, like this, and he stabs himself in the leg. And I don't know that he felt it too much that night. And I looked at it. I said, let me see, you know. It was -- it was slit about the width of the knife blade, and -- but -- but it was laid over, you know, like they do, like they peel -- peel over, closed at the ends, but kind of oval shape now. And he was bleeding, and I thought, geez. Well, anyhow, Louie lived in the direction we were going from the Corner Cafe, and he says, come, come, you come, come. So he directed us to his house. And somebody in that house had just had a baby, and they had diapers and towels and everything, and he ended up in there and I'm taking care of it with this diaper. And I'll never forget the -- one the women said, good doctor, good doctor, to me, I'm a good doctor. So, anyhow, I dressed as best I could and tied this diaper around it, and we went on back to camp. That thing -- he wasn't in lineup in the morning. He -- no, he was not in lineup in the morning. I guess that thing had gotten really sore, stiffened up on him. He had to go to medics, and all that stuff, but just neat little stories. Something like the one I was telling last night about -- but that has nothing to do with your --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you mentioned that one -- the big loss with the losing that gun and all those guys. Did you lose any close buddies over there?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: No. It was a different battery. That was A Battery. We were C Battery. We were -- our truck was right behind that thing. We were all in pretty -- we stopped for a -- for a call, and we were pulled over and -- and stationary when the thing came in and blammed. Yeah, it was not nice.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you didn't really get close to guys in the other batteries, you kind of --

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Oh --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- stayed with your group?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Oh, yeah. You -- you -- you were -- in our bunch, in our battalion, you were probably closest to the men in your section because you lived with them and you worked with them, and whatever, but, oh, I had a -- I had a nice variety. I had a -- a real good friend in the machine -- Essie was in the machine gun section, and another fellow that was on the guns was very close, too, and this -- a guy on the radar, which wasn't too far away from our direction -- director. You formed your circle of friends just like you do here, but it didn't -- didn't go beyond a battery. You didn't have anybody out of the battery that you were friendly with, did you?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: I don't think so.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: I had -- I had a fellow that would -- ended up being in B Battery that I rode from -- from Fort Hayes all the way out to California side by side, but he -- you didn't know, but he ended up in B Battery and I was in C Battery, and, yeah, you were -- you weren't enemies with them, but you never -- you never had an opportunity to be really close to them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How many men were in a battery?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: I -- 150, was it?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: About 150.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: 135, 150, somewhere in there.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: I -- one of our buddies is -- is down here at Heather Hill (ph) right now, and oddly enough, he's been very active in our association. We have a 125th AAA Gun Battalion Association, and he was very active in that, in that he -- he would come to anything that we had every year (for) reunion. We had a -- I invented a pre-union party that we had down at Dabromex (ph) that we had every year, and he was always on hand with his wife, and he was in a wheelchair. I don't know that -- that he was -- that his wheelchair experience was -- was army related, but anyhow, he ended up in a wheelchair, and his wife was a great caretaker of -- of him. Anyhow, this past before July -- before our July reunion, we found out that his wife had a heart attack, and they had just been to the pre-union party with us. It was my job to dance with her every time we got together because he couldn't dance. It was with his permission. So, anyhow, we -- we found out that Ruth had had a heart attack, and at that time, we found out that Glen had had a heart attack, too. It seems that Ruth had a heart attack in the morning, they got her to a hospital and into a room, and Glen and his -- one of his kids came back home to his house, where he had a heart attack. They both had heart attacks the same day. And, well, we lost Ruth. Ruth, Ruth didn't survive it, but Glen had a triple bypass, and he's down at Heather Hill and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What's Glen's last name?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Lindstrom.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I've interviewed him.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Did you really?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I sure have.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Oh, good. Good for you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I thought that's who you were talking about.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Oh, yes. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He was living up in Medderoff (ph) _____+?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Oh, really? Sure.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. Yeah, exactly.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Yeah. He had -- we stopped over to -- to see how he was doing. We were a little late doing this, but it was hard to do.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when did Ruth die?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Oh, do you know the date?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was it recently, within the last year, or whatever?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female Speaker
sp.p: It was in May, or something. It was this year.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It was in May?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Was she still alive when you --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, because I talked to him, boy, a year-and-a-half or two years ago, whatever. It was when I -- shortly after I started doing this, I talked to Glen.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Oh, the --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How long has he been in Heather Hill?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Three, four months.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female Speaker
sp.p: He went there after he had open-heart surgery.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He went there after his surgery?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female Speaker
sp.p: Yes. They put him there after that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, I probably talked to him in -- yeah, it's almost two years ago now, almost. Been more than a year-and-a-half since I talked to Glen.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Oh, he was still in Mentor then.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He was still in Mentor, right. Exactly.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: And his wife, everything was fine then.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. Yeah, exactly.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Okay. Because this -- we -- we visited him, what, two, three weeks ago, and the -- he was better than I thought he was going to be, but he was out of his wheelchair. His wheelchair was there, but he was in bed, said -- complained about his back hurting.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: He was restricted to -- to bed for one reason or another.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female Speaker
sp.p: Bed sores. He had really bad bed sores.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Oh, was it bed sores? And wasn't able to get into his wheelchair and -- but we were visiting and -- and he says, Al, he says, I got some pictures of the whole battalion. He says, would you want them. He says, they're in my garage. And I said, sure. I've got an -- I've got a picture of our battery, but I didn't want to turn him down for anything. I said, oh, heck yes, Glen, I'd love to have them. But anyhow, his daughter dropped them off here just a couple days ago --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: -- and there's five pictures he's got. And I took -- Dino and I go to spaghetti, and our wives go to spaghetti every Monday night over here at Alysse's (ph), so I took one of the pictures over there this past Monday night. We -- we went over to Dairy Queen after spaghetti, put it out on the table there. We were sitting there talking about that and pointing to this guy and that guy for a good 45 minutes or more. It was -- they had a picture of -- the reason I took it was because there was -- there was a picture of me in that thing that I didn't even know existed. I don't remember sitting for it, or whatever. But for a little while at -- when -- just before we were -- went overseas, when we were at Camp Edwards in Massachusetts, they wanted to form up a drum and bugle corp, and -- and I played the drums, so, okay, I stuck my name in there. And I don't remember any reference to that from then on, as far as the outfit is concerned, but right in that headquarters battery picture, there's me sitting in the front row with the rest of the drummers; there's five of us. And I thought, when the hell did they take that. That's me, you know. At last I can show the kids I was in the drum and bugle corp, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, I probably saw this picture a year-and-a-half ago, too. He was showing me a lot of stuff.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Oh, I'll bet you did. Yeah, they -- they're long and plastic-enclosed.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Hell, he wouldn't have known me in that, though. But --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: -- anyhow, we had a great deal of fun with that. Now we're -- now we're going to try to reproduce just the drum and bugle corp of that thing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: And I didn't know until I took it in to show my son, to show him, see that, I was in there, he says, what do those guys got under their arms up there. And looked at it, he said -- I said, what do you mean. They -- they had their bugles parked like this.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: It was the whole drum and bugle corp.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: When I took that picture in there, it was just the drum corp --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: -- but when I got it in to my son --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: -- somebody had stuck the bugle corp in there, too --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: -- all -- all the way up the _____+. Well, it's fun.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Other than the fact that the British couldn't shoot straight, did you get along with them?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: No. Hell, no. No. Damn Limies.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Damn Limies. Are you kidding? Well, we'd go in -- when we were in -- in Nijlen, we'd go in and get Cognac. They'd sit there and sip on lemonade -- lemonade, they called it. No, we'd -- we had a guy in our outfit, Maynard. Remember Maynard?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: He was -- well, he was a hillbilly. I -- I'm sure he was, but he was a nice guy. Nice -- nice appearing, just a -- a nice guy. And we'd be sitting around, and he'd nudge somebody like this and say, hey, hell, let's go in and beat up on a couple of Limies. Let's go beat up on a couple Limies. He was tough. No, we didn't get along well with them at all. For -- for the main -- the main reason for that is that we got along with their women better than they got along with their women. We were -- we were higher paid, we were more well off, wealthier, higher paid. And it was -- it was strange, and I'll -- I'll -- I'll repeat this for the rest of my life, that you could understand the women. The British girls, you could understand what they were saying. The British guys, you couldn't understand them. It was like a foreign language. Isn't that odd?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female Speaker
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Did you find that, Dino?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Oh, I had a hard time.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: You can't understand them. They'd {made sound} like this. Well, what the hell did you say? But the -- the gals, it was just like talking to -- to you, or to anyone.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: But the ones that were educated, you could understand them well.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Oh, you mean the -- the rest of them were not educated?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Well, I don't know, there -- they must have a dialect, or something.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Were the girls educated and the guys not? I guess that that must be it.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Well, I think they had a certain dialect that you have a hard time understanding.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: And it wasn't the obvious reason that you wanted to understand the girls more than the guys, but you just could.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: If you talked to a British girl, it was just like talking to a girl back home. But you talk to the guy, and -- you're not English, are you?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: The guys, it was like a foreign tongue. Strange.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Our guys had a laugh when they had -- they always had a tea break.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Oh, yeah, break for tea.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: They'd have a tea break. They'd stop everything and have tea.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: They -- they were a different cut. They -- their country was even different.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: You know, we used to laugh at their tea break. Now our guys have a coffee break, now. We never used to have that before.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: The -- their country was -- was backward compared to the Belgian peoples, or the German people. We got along -- we -- this -- this was commonly said, that we got along better with the German PW's than we got along with those Limies, and we were always going to sink that damn island on the way back home. This -- this was the talk, wasn't it?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Yep. No, we didn't get along with them at all. We got along real well with the German PW's.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you responsible for guarding some of the German PW's?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Yes, sometime.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: We guarded them.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: At one point, I can remember doing that. They had the most -- they were all -- I can remember them being in tents, and I can remember their -- their walkways and everything was just impeccable. Their -- the little garden, they'd have a little garden planted out in -- in front. Everything was just right up to snuff, and, well, England wasn't quite like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember a mail call, getting letters, packages from home, that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Sure, especially that Golden Wedding, but don't tell.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was the best?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Shh, don't tell anybody.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Everybody lined up for mail call --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you write a lot back to -- to family?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Did I write a lot?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: I have all the letters that my mother wrote to me --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: -- from there. Those are kind of tough to look at, but --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female Speaker
sp.p: I thought those were the ones that you wrote to her.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Oh, that's right. They're the ones that I wrote to her. She saved all the letters that I wrote to her. That's why it's so hard --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: You know, talking about --

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: -- I can't read my writing.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Talking about mail call, I didn't write home too often, and apparently my mother went to the Red Cross and complained about it. And somehow the Red Cross got a hold of our outfit and our captain found out about this. And at night, we used to seal the letters that he's censored -- all the letters were censored. He'd read them, and then he'd give us the letters, and we'd seal them up. So one night, he writes -- starts writing on a piece of paper and he comes to me, said Rondini (ph), I started this letter for your mother, you finish it. Well, I thought that was pretty -- he was pretty caring, you know. He -- he worried about us guys.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: That's the -- that's the guy I told you was still alive, our captain.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. Right.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Well, I'll tell you something about him, when we were in service, when we first met him and all the way through, that guy looked like a giant.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Today, come on, he -- he's -- he's no bigger than we are, really. Well, maybe a little bit, but, boy, he -- he was like -- you probably don't even remember Punjab, but Pun --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, I --

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: -- punjab was in Little Andy Rooney or Orphan Annie, or something like that. He looked like Punjab in those days, a great big raw-boned plow jockey from --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: And he had a really -- a commanding voice.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: He had big voice, oh --

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Slow, slowly talked.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: He said something, you -- you'd do it.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: He had a glower about him. Still has a glower. He still has a glower, but he isn't big enough to back it up anymore.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Another thing he'd do --

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: He was a hell of a nice guy. Really, he was.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: -- we didn't have a -- I was Catholic.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: We didn't have a Catholic priest in our outfit, we had Protestant. So the captain gave the guys a truck -- this was -- was when we were in France. He gave the guys a truck to go to a Catholic church, and so I'm -- I'm right there, you know, I'm on duty. He says, Rondini, aren't you going to church? I said, Captain, I'm on duty, I can't go to church. He said, you go to church, I'm going to take your place, and he sent me to church.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Good grief.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Yeah, he was a good one. That's why C Battery was the best battery in the battalion, because of him.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: We all had a lot of respect for him and --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: We weren't with the officers all the time, their -- the -- our computer was the C.P. --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: -- and all the orders would come from there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you got along with your officers, for the most part?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: I think so.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: There were a couple -- couple we didn't think too much of, but they all -- they all had us in their hearts, I guess.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So after the Bulge, you said you were doing, what, mainly MP work, and that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: They made us MP's, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When did you finally come home?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: When they let us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When did you have enough points?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was it late in '45, or --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female Speaker
sp.p: It was in June, wasn't it?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: June? Oh, that's not too bad. An extra month after V-E Day. Was there a possibility you were going to be sent to the war in --

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: The war ended.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Against Japan?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Didn't the war end? The war ended, didn't it?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, if you --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: No. Well --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- came back in June, it was still going --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: The war was still going.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- in the Pacific.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: They did ask us, would you prefer to stay here in Europe, or would you prefer to go to Japan. And my -- my answer was I -- I'd sooner go to Japan, because I figured when you stay in Europe, there's no war or nothing, and they're pretty strict with you, you know. You have -- you have to polish your shoes, and everything, and make sure you're shaved, so I said I -- I'll go to Japan. And not only that, when you go to Japan, you go through the United States and you -- you get a furlough first, so -- but then _____+.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Little method in your madness, huh?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, what, like a 30-day break in the States before they would ship you out to the Pacific?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Well, most guys were shipped to the United States, get a furlough, and then go over -- over to Japan.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: I came home and I was discharged right away.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Oh, yeah. The war was over then.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Oh, it ended while we were on -- on our way home?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, it depends. Did you say you came home in June, or did you --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: No, we came home in February.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: February '45, or '46?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Oh, god, I got to figure that out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, if it was February '45, the war was still going in Europe.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Forty-five, well, that was in June, right, '45?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The war in Europe ended in May of '45.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Okay. Then it was the same year, then, Japan ended.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. In August?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: So --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So maybe when you were en route back to the States?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: No, the war was all -- already --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Already over by the time you got back? Oh, okay. So it must have been sometime after August when you were --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: I was discharged in February. You were, too.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Oh, I was? Like I say, once the past, it's past.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you in the army of occupation for considerable amount of time, then, or --

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Not that you remember?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Well, from June --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: From June until when you came back?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: -- until we came back.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay. So that would make sense, probably, that it would have been February '46 when you were discharged.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: No, when we were discharged, it was early '46.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Never forget that trip home.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Never forget that trip home. They put us on a -- we -- we crossed on the -- on a great big huge ocean liner, and with sun decks, and we formed a little band on the poop deck back there and played, you know, just relaxing, having a good time.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female Speaker
sp.p: I don't think that's it. That says '49.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: February -- well, whatever. And they marched us over to the piers, there, and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: -- there was this damn little boat. We had a three- or four-stacker going over. The _____ of the boat had about one-and-a-half stacks on it, and it was called the Sea Robin. We got on board, and they took us down and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: There you go, February '46.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: -- they took us down below decks, past these damn oven steamers -- whatever the hell they were, but terrible odor below deck -- and they gave us a --a dish, like beef stew, stroganoff, maybe. Thick gravy, chunks of beef, cubed pieces of beef in it. Well, of course we were hungry, so we ate. And no sooner got that down and they let the darn thing go, and we're out to sea. We're going out to sea, it's February on the Atlantic Ocean. I was up toward the bow of the boat. There was a bare light bulb hanging down, illuminating cots strung up the side maybe five or six high, and that boat was just pitching and rolling. They had -- they -- every -- everything was billowed up. They closed all the hatches because the boat was plowing through like that. And up in front, there, we -- we were getting quite a ride. This thing would pitch under the waves, and go up like this, and just smack down onto the ocean. And some of the guys -- you -- you might find this hard to believe, but some of the guys were getting a little bit ill, and they'd -- they'd roll over like this. And these pipe frames that these cots were stretched across, they'd -- they'd toss their cookies, and it would just kind of -- you ever seen it slime down like this from -- from one thing to another, and then go {made sound} like this, and then on down? Well, that was going on, and I stood it for as long as I could. And believe it or not, I was starting to get feeling sick, so I just added to the -- the last blob that went down, I just kind of added a little bit to, and it just kind of slopped down. And we -- nobody was talking, or nobody was cracking-wise, or anything. It was just -- everybody was miserable as hell. So I thought, I can't stand it here anymore, I got to get someplace. And I reached my hand over, and -- and, oops. But -- but you got to -- you have to do that, because you can't just roll off the third bunk up and smack on the floor. So, okay, all right, get down, and you step down on the thing and -- and there's a double stairway going over there with these steel treads --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: -- for the steps with -- with beef mashed between them all. They reach up and -- and grab hold of the handrail to go up. And you can't get a real good hold on it because it's so damn slippery with vomit, and somehow got to the -- and the odor, too, the odor below decks, all closed up, no ventilation or anything, it just wreaked with -- with barf. So, anyhow, finally got up to the top and followed some guys that were headed to the head. And it was a big square room, white porcelain tiles in the floor, with that shit mashed between them, again. And they had a big -- they had toilets down one -- stools -- stools down one side, and the other side had a big long urinal. And as the ship would leap like this, you'd get a -- they were all stopped up, of course, and you'd get this wave of puke going. You could see it just going down there and {made sound} against the wall and onto the floor, and I'll tell you --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female Speaker
sp.p: You love to tell that story.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Well, it -- it's so vivid, Dear. It's so vivid in my mind, I will never be able to forget that.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Female Speaker
sp.p: You're trying to make it that way for us.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: The -- the toilets, of course, the stools were all brimming, too, and they'd slop off like this. Not -- but that big wave just {made sound}. Then the floor was so slippery you had to hold on to some damn thing. You couldn't -- you couldn't make it across this big room without going on your ass. Wouldn't that have been something? So, anyhow, that wasn't much help. And they couldn't get up to get a breath of fresh air, we were just {made sound}, everything's closed. The crew was sick, everybody on that ship was sick. Why in the world did they give you a dish like that to -- to leave on? But, anyhow, it went. I -- I'll bet -- the guys were worried about me, because I did have some friends. Webby was -- Webby was on my boat, and his friend, that red-haired guy. Anyhow, they decided that they would save me and urge me to get out of that bunk, because I was just in there. I wasn't going to get out of that for anything. I was in there for four days just {made sound}. And anyhow, they came and, come on, Al, you got to get something to eat, and they urged me up and on my feet. Otherwise, I'd still be on that damn thing. I'd never, never had an experience like that in my whole life. Never want it again. Not -- not too crazy to get on a -- on a cruise.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Although, we did ride the Jet Express up there at (Footlin) Bay -- that was fun -- this past weekend. Not this past weekend, weekend before.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when you think about the war, do any other vivid memories come to mind?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Oh, hard to -- I think we've pretty much covered the thing end to end. I'm sure there are other ones, if I sat and thought about it real hard, but --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: We've covered it?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Yeah. Can you add anything? It's pretty hard to pinpoint anything in the middle, there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Well, when we were -- before we were -- we went on the -- on the ship to come home, we weren't -- we were in Le Havre, and, of course, you line up when you get, you know, your food bit, and you fill up your mess kit. And a lot of times the food wasn't too good. And then they have garbage cans where you throw the -- the waste food, you know, that we ain't finished. And I got sick when I -- these French people didn't have no food, and they'd go in the garbage can and scoop up the -- the food that we threw away. That made me sick.

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Well, I don't see anything wrong with that.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: You didn't see that?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Well, I don't really see anything wrong with that. I mean, it wasn't --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: In the -- in the garbage -- garbage can?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Yeah, but it wasn't --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: The stuff you threw away? It's all mixed up and everything. Oh --

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: Yeah, but it wasn't vomit.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: No, but --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You love that vomit, huh?

sp.speaker: Alvin Harry Wedler
sp.p: It was all stuff that they had given you to eat, so it couldn't have been terrible.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: I had never saw that before. Yeah, exactly. I never have saw it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Oh --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They were starving?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Male Speaker
sp.p: Yeah. That -- that bothered me.
[END OF INTERVIEW]
